callouts.text: The two figures the client actually watches, with the change against today's baseline. Read from the harness output; nothing on this page is a number somebody typed in.
The kill switch. Halting writes a file, and the next ticket routes on R-00 and goes to a person with its draft attached. No deployment, and nothing in flight is lost.
Eight real tickets, each chosen because it takes a different route through the rules. The chip on each says which rule will fire before you click it.
The routing decision. The rule that made it, and the reason in the words a support manager would use rather than an engineer.
Intent, with a calibrated confidence: the probability this prediction is correct, not the softmax mass on the winning class. The bar is marked at the routing threshold.
The retrieved passages with their BM25 scores. The cited one is open, showing the actual article text the citation resolves to. That is acceptance criterion A6, checked by eye.
The reply as it would be sent. The [1] marker lights up the passage it came from, and the closing paragraph tells the customer a machine drafted it.
A security incident, recognised with 100% confidence, and escalated anyway. R-01 is a policy rule: no confidence is high enough for this class. That is the whole design in one line.
Latency, the threshold that was applied, and which generator produced the text. All three are written to the decision log.
The classification is confident and correct. It is not what decided the outcome, which is the point of putting policy ahead of confidence.
The handover note. Daniel, the tier two engineer, asked for exactly this: what the customer wants, what documentation looked relevant, and what the system was unsure about.
The articles were retrieved and deliberately not sent. They travel with the escalation so the engineer does not start from a blank page.
